citation: Sonjon et al. (2025), BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders
title: Social factors contributing to the development of chronic low back pain: a scoping review
authors: Yvan Sonjon; Annabelle Gonthier; Camille Lépingle; Jean-Baptiste Van der Henst; Karen T. Reilly; Eric Chabanat
pain_condition_detail: non-specific chronic low back pain (CLBP), defined as pain in the lumbar region present for at least 3 months
context_note: Focused on industrialized Western countries; includes primary, secondary, and tertiary care settings.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; justification; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the BPS model as an organizing principle to scope social factors in CLBP. It defines social factors broadly as external influences, reclassifies some biological/psychological factors as socially shaped, and proposes a six-domain classification. No cross-domain mechanisms are specified; integration is absent.
integration_mechanism_summary: None proposed. The paper describes associations between social factors and psychological constructs (e.g., depression mediating social status and pain, stress mediating income and pain) but specifies no pathways or processes.
emergent_labels_4: MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status
conceptual_tensions_1: Paper reclassifies biological/psychological factors as social (e.g., BMI, sleep) but does not specify mechanisms linking them to social determinants
conceptual_tensions_2: Claims BPS model involves 'complex interactions' but only lists social factors in parallel, no cross-domain integration is provided
conceptual_tensions_3: Acknowledges boundary issues between BPS domains but does not resolve them, uses broad definition of social factors that may dilute specificity
additional_observations_1: The paper is a scoping review that explicitly focuses on social factors, with minimal biological and psychological content. It uses BPS as an organizing principle to justify its scope but does not integrate domains
additional_observations_2: The classification system (six domains) is the main contribution, it is descriptive and does not propose causal pathways
additional_observations_3: The paper critiques the literature for treating social factors as adjustment variables rather than explanatory ones, but does not itself model them as such
synthesis_note: This scoping review provides a comprehensive classification of social factors in CLBP (28 categories, 6 domains) but does not integrate biological, psychological, and social domains. BPS is used as an organizing principle; no mechanisms or pathways are specified. The paper is social-dominant with minimal biological and psychological coverage, illustrating a common pattern of BPS language without substantive integration.
coding_rationale: Typology 'pseudo_bps' because BPS language is used but biological and psychological domains are thin. Triadic integration is 'none' as domains are listed in parallel. Social domain is elaborated; biological and psychological are minimal/mentioned.

title: Social factors contributing to the development of chronic low back pain: a scoping review
authors: Yvan Sonjon; Annabelle Gonthier; Camille Lépingle; Jean-Baptiste Van der Henst; Karen T. Reilly; Eric Chabanat
pain_condition_detail: Adult non-specific chronic low back pain (CLBP), defined as lumbar pain for at least 3 months after acute causes/treatments have been addressed.
context_note: Industrialized Western countries with comparable relational, cultural, political frameworks and healthcare structures/delivery models; WEIRD limitation noted.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; operational definition; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: It uses BPS chiefly to define social factors as external influences and to classify 28 categories into six domains. Biological and psychological factors are included only when socially shaped; pairwise pathways are cited, but no triadic mechanism is modeled.
integration_mechanism_summary: No three-domain mechanism proposed. It proposes social determinants shaping lifestyle/health indicators and stigma affecting care access, and psychosocial mediators such as depression and perceived stress linking social conditions to pain outcomes; biological, psychological, and social factors are not modeled as a single system.
emergent_labels_4: patient’s experience of health care domain
emergent_labels_9: MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status
emergent_labels_12: health literacy specific to low back pain
conceptual_tensions_1: BPS is used to justify social-factor inclusion, but the review’s own synthesis is mainly descriptive classification rather than mechanism
conceptual_tensions_2: Biological or psychological factors are reclassified as social when socially shaped, creating a debatable boundary between domains
conceptual_tensions_3: Social relationships are described as important for recovery, yet family and professional support remain underexplored
conceptual_tensions_4: Social factors are often treated as adjustment variables or economic impacts rather than explanatory contributors to CLBP progression
conceptual_tensions_5: Western WEIRD restriction may underrepresent marginalized populations and systemic or cultural injustice
additional_observations_1: The review explicitly states that included studies used a BPS model, but its own synthesis is a descriptive classification of social factors
additional_observations_2: No critical appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment was conducted because the authors judged it inappropriate for the scoping-review aim
additional_observations_3: The review says its reclassification of biological or psychological factors as social is descriptive and does not reinterpret original findings
additional_observations_4: The paper recommends mixed methods and participatory action research for underrepresented domains
additional_observations_5: The review calls for hypothesis-driven research to test temporal and potentially causal links between social factors and CLBP evolution
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mainly as a social lens for CLBP. It elaborates social and psychosocial factors, mentions biological/lifestyle factors when socially shaped, and uses BPS to justify classification and care strategies. It names pairwise pathways, especially social-psychological mediators, but does not model a three-domain system.
coding_rationale: Social-dominant pseudo-BPS: BPS organizes the review and care rationale, but biological content is thin and triadic integration is absent.

citation: Sonjon et al. (2025), BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders
title: Social factors contributing to the development of chronic low back pain: a scoping review
authors: Yvan Sonjon; Annabelle Gonthier; Camille Lépingle; Jean-Baptiste Van der Henst; Karen T. Reilly; Eric Chabanat
bps_function_set: background framing; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: Organizes the review into six social domains (socio-demographic, socio-occupational, socio-environmental, global health data, psycho-social, patient experience of healthcare) and categorizes 28 factor types, treating biological and psychological factors as socially shaped rather than maintaining distinct domains.
integration_mechanism_summary: Three directional claims: depression mediates social status to pain severity; perceived stress mediates household income to pain persistence; social support influences self-efficacy affecting CLBP outcomes. No biological domain integration proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS theoretical framework and practical treatment of biological and psychological factors as socially shaped
conceptual_tensions_2: Gap between BPS label usage and actual integration of three domains in CLBP research
conceptual_tensions_3: Underrepresentation of interpersonal and family-level social factors despite their recognized importance
additional_observations_1: Review focuses exclusively on social factors, treating biological and psychological factors as socially determined rather than maintaining distinct domains
additional_observations_2: Classification system organizes 28 factor categories into 6 social domains, with Global Health Data domain including traditionally biological factors (BMI, sleep) re-conceptualized as social
additional_observations_3: No formal quality appraisal conducted, consistent with scoping review methodology but limits ability to assess strength of evidence
additional_observations_4: Citation network analysis reveals fragmented literature with limited cross-citation between studies
synthesis_note: This scoping review operationalizes the BPS model by organizing social factors into six domains and 28 categories, treating biological and psychological factors as socially shaped. It identifies significant gaps in social factor research, particularly for interpersonal relationships, and critiques current clinical assessment tools for inadequately capturing social dimensions. The review demonstrates how BPS language can serve as an organizing principle while substantive three-domain integration remains absent.
coding_rationale: Scored social domain as elaborated due to 28 factor categories organized into 6 domains; psychological as mentioned due to 9 named constructs; biological as absent. Triadic integration scored as none due to absence of biological domain. BPS typology as multifactorial because all three domains present but social dominates. Integration claims identified 3 directional relationships between psychological and social factors.
